messages.content: I've been looking through the vscode codebase to see how we might implement a proper tabbed interface. I noticed the current implementation in src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/editor/editor.ts seems to rely heavily on a single-tab view. I want to move towards a multi-tab system. Where should I start looking for the core editor container logic?

That is an ambitious goal. You should start by examining src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/editor/tabsTitleControl.ts, which handles the rendering of the tab headers. Currently, it is quite rudimentary. You will also need to investigate src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/editor/editorGroupView.ts to understand how individual editors are housed. The main challenge will be managing the state of multiple tabs and ensuring that the editor group can handle a list of input descriptors rather than just one active editor.

I see. I've been experimenting with adding a tabs collection to EditorGroupView. When I try to update the tab count, I'm hitting a runtime error in the layout logic inside editorPart.ts. It seems like the height calculation for the breadcrumbs is failing when I have more than one tab open, as the DOM elements aren't being updated correctly. Any ideas on why the reflow is failing?

That sounds like a classic CSS layout issue within the Workbench. If you look at src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/editor/editorPart.css, you'll see the layout constraints are hardcoded to a single header. You need to adjust the flex-basis properties to accommodate the new tab row. Also, check if your update call is triggering an layout() event in the editor contribution. You might need to manually call layout() after the DOM injection in tabsTitleControl.ts.

Good catch on the CSS. After updating the flexbox properties, the tabs are rendering, but clicking them doesn't switch the editor context. I am seeing 'Cannot read property 'group' of undefined' when I call editorService.openEditor inside tabsTitleControl.ts. It seems my reference to the active editor group is stale during the tab change event. How is the group lifecycle managed?

The editor group lifecycle is managed by the EditorGroupService. In your case, it seems you are losing the context of the group when the tab switch triggers. Verify that you are passing the correct EditorGroup object into your tabsTitleControl instance upon creation. Look at how editorGroupView.ts instantiates the title control and ensure the group reference is injected via the constructor, rather than relying on a global accessor which might be out of sync.

I fixed the lifecycle issue by using a proper service injection for the IEditorGroupService. Now, clicking tabs successfully switches the editor. However, the 'rip a tab out' feature is proving difficult. I'm trying to implement drag-and-drop using the standard HTML5 DragEvent, but the Electron process is blocking the drop target. Do I need to hook into the custom vscode dnd service?

Yes, standard HTML5 DragEvent behavior is often constrained within the Electron shell. You should look at src/vs/base/browser/ui/list/listView.ts to see how we handle drag operations for the explorer and use that same approach. Specifically, look into the DragAndDropController in src/vs/workbench/browser/dnd.ts. You need to register your tab element as a valid drop target in the workbench service to allow external drops and window splitting.

Implementing the drag-and-drop using the workbench DND controller helped, but I'm getting an error when I try to open a new window with the detached tab: 'Error: Cannot create a new window with the provided editor input.' It seems the serialized state of the IEditorInput isn't fully supported across BrowserWindow instances. Is there a serialization layer I should be using?

You are running into the limitations of the current workspace state. For cross-window communication, you must use the IEditorInputSerializer interface defined in src/vs/workbench/common/editor.ts. Ensure your input type implements serialize() and that it is registered in the EditorInputRegistry. Once it is serializable to JSON, you can pass the state to the main process via the IPC bridge, which will then instruct the main process to open a new BrowserWindow instance.

I've implemented the serializer, but now the new window opens as an empty instance, ignoring the input. I checked the IPC logs, and the serialized payload seems correct, but it's not being parsed on the other side. Is the Workbench initialized with the input state early enough during the startup sequence in main.ts?

Ah, the issue is that the Workbench initialization in main.ts happens asynchronously. You need to intercept the 'open-editor' event in the secondary process before the editorPart.ts is fully realized. Check how we handle command-line arguments in src/vs/code/electron-main/main.ts. You might need to add a command line argument or a specific startup flag to pass the serialized editor state so it can be restored during the startup of the second window.

That makes sense. I added a --open-editor-state flag to the main startup arguments and hooked it into the environmentService. The window is now opening with the content, but the tab styling is missing in the new window. It looks like the theme service isn't applying correctly to the new window instance. Is there a race condition with the CSS loading?

It is possible that the ThemeService is trying to inject styles before the DOM is ready. Try wrapping your CSS application logic in a requestIdleCallback or checking the status of the IThemeService.onThemeChange event. Also, verify that the 'workbench.desktop.main.css' file is being correctly bundled for secondary windows in your build configuration in build/gulpfile.vscode.js.

I verified the CSS bundle, and everything is there. It turns out I had a small bug in my CSS variable injection where I was referencing the theme colors before the theme had actually finished loading. Adding a listener to IThemeService.onThemeChange in editorGroupView.ts fixed it. The tabs now look correct in the detached window. What's the best way to handle dragging a tab back into the main window?

To merge windows, you need a global drag-and-drop monitor that exists across all browser windows. Since that is complex, a simpler approach is to use the IWindowService to detect when a tab is dragged near another window's boundary. When that happens, you can trigger a cross-window move event. You will need to use an IPC message to 'close' the tab in the child window and 'open' it in the parent window simultaneously to ensure a smooth transition.

That sounds feasible. I've started building the cross-window IPC listener, but I'm getting a 'Connection reset by peer' error when I try to transfer large editor inputs between processes. Is there a limit on the size of the data I can send over IPC?

Electron's IPC has a limit for large objects because they are serialized as strings. For large editor inputs, you should avoid passing the full state via IPC. Instead, use the IFileService to save the temporary state to a file on disk in the temp directory, send the file path over IPC, and have the target window read the state from that file. This is much more stable for large payloads.

Using the file system as a bridge worked perfectly and eliminated the IPC size errors. I have basic tab management and detachment working now. I still have some flickering when switching tabs rapidly. I noticed that the tabsTitleControl.ts does a full re-render on every tab change. How can I optimize this to only update the active tab state?

Instead of a full re-render, you should implement a virtualized list for the tabs. Look at src/vs/base/browser/ui/list/listWidget.ts and see if you can refactor your tab container to act like a list. By only updating the class names of the tabs (e.g., adding 'active' or 'inactive' CSS classes) rather than recreating the DOM nodes, you should see a significant performance boost and eliminate the flickering. Great progress on this feature.

I've refactored the tabsTitleControl.ts to use a list-like approach, but now the context menus on the tabs are broken. It seems like the event delegation in the ListWidget is swallowing the context menu events. How should I properly bubble these up for the tab items?

You need to override the 'onContextMenu' handler in your custom list renderer. Instead of letting the ListWidget handle it exclusively, ensure you propagate the 'ContextMenuEvent' to your workbench's context menu service, specifically the IContextMenuService, so it can resolve the correct actions for the tab.

That worked. I registered the context menu service in the list renderer, and the menus are now showing up correctly. However, I've noticed a new issue where dragging a tab causes the entire tab bar to shift layout. It seems the placeholder calculation in tabsTitleControl.ts isn't accounting for the margin collapsed by the list widget.

Margin collapse is a classic CSS headache in these UI layouts. Check the 'tabSizing' configuration in your css file. You may need to set 'overflow: hidden' on the container or explicitly calculate the width including the margins before passing it to the ListWidget's layout engine.

Adding explicit width calculation in the layout loop fixed the layout shift. Now, I want to handle 'Save All' across multiple windows. If I trigger this in the main window, it currently only saves files in the main window's scope. How do I broadcast this to the secondary windows?

You need to use the 'IWindowsMainService' in the main process to iterate over all active code windows. Broadcast a 'vscode:saveAll' event to all windows via 'webContents.send'. Then, have each secondary window listen for this event and call 'editorService.saveAll()'.

The broadcast is working, but the saving is synchronous and blocks the main process, causing the UI to hang for a split second during heavy file writes. Should I offload these save calls to the worker threads?

Exactly. Avoid blocking the main process loop. Use an 'async' call to the file service, and perhaps look into the 'IWorkingCopyService' to perform non-blocking saves. This ensures the main window stays responsive while the secondary windows handle their own I/O.

I've offloaded the saves to the worker thread using the 'IWorkingCopyService'. It's much smoother now. I’m now turning my attention to keyboard shortcuts. Ctrl+Tab to cycle through tabs only works within the focused window. How do I make this work globally across all tabbed windows?

Keyboard shortcuts are typically scoped to the focused workbench. To make it global, you'd need to intercept the keybinding in the main process and check which window currently has focus. If you want a 'cycle-next-window' behavior, you'll need to maintain a registry of window IDs in an array.

I've created a 'windowRegistry.ts' to track focus. When Ctrl+Tab is pressed, the main process now determines the next window in the list and calls 'window.focus()'. It works, but it feels a bit jarring. Is there a way to make the focus switch feel more native?

The jarring effect often comes from the lack of a window animation. Try using 'window.show()' or ensure 'window.focus()' is triggered after the previous window has relinquished control. You might also check if there is an Electron native hook for 'bringToFront' which is sometimes smoother.

Switching to 'bringToFront' definitely helped. I'm hitting a snag with the 'Close Window' command. When I close a window, the tab state is lost. I need to make sure the editor state is persisted to the global storage before the window actually unloads.

Listen to the 'onBeforeUnload' event in your workbench class. Inside that handler, trigger an asynchronous save to your serialized storage. You should also ensure the main process receives a confirmation signal before finalizing the 'window.close()' call to prevent data loss.

I implemented the 'onBeforeUnload' listener. I'm using a 'Promise' to delay the close until the persistence logic completes. It seems robust, but I'm worried about users force-quitting the app. Is there a way to auto-save periodically?

For that, implement a 'DebouncedScheduler' that triggers a background save every 30 seconds. In 'workbench.ts', you can register this scheduler to run automatically as long as the window is active. This will minimize data loss in case of a crash.

The auto-save is working well. Now, the final hurdle: window-to-window drag and drop. I'm trying to use the native HTML5 Drag and Drop API, but it's not working across different Electron processes. Are there limitations there?

The native HTML5 DND API is isolated to a single renderer process. For cross-window DND, you need to use the Electron 'ipcRenderer' and 'ipcMain' to simulate a DND 'proxy' window that follows the mouse cursor while it's in between windows.

A proxy window is a smart workaround. I'll create a transparent, click-through overlay window that tracks the cursor position. I can then use the 'drag-start' and 'drag-end' events in the main process to handle the handoff.

That is the standard pattern for custom DND in multi-window desktop apps. Once the cursor enters the target window's bounds, send the payload via IPC to the target window and 'close' the proxy window. This should provide a seamless tab-ripping experience.

I've successfully set up the proxy window, but I'm struggling with the hit detection. When I drag the tab out, the proxy window triggers, but the target window doesn't seem to register the 'drag-over' event when I release the mouse. Is this an issue with the transparent window's 'ignore-mouse-events' flag?

Exactly. If your proxy window has 'setIgnoreMouseEvents(true)' enabled, it effectively becomes invisible to the operating system's event loop, preventing it from tracking drag progress. You need to toggle this flag dynamically. Set it to true when the mouse leaves the proxy area, and false when the drag session is active.

That fixed the tracking issue. However, now I see a flickering white frame around the proxy window while dragging. I am using 'frame: false' and 'transparent: true' in the 'BrowserWindow' options. Is there a way to suppress the frame entirely during the drag transition?

The flickering is likely caused by the OS re-rendering the shadow layer when the window state updates. Try setting 'hasShadow: false in your BrowserWindow constructor for the proxy. Additionally, ensure you are using 'backgroundColor: #00000000' to explicitly notify Electron that the frame should be fully transparent.

Setting 'hasShadow' to false definitely cleaned up the visuals. Now, when I drop the tab into the new window, the tab content flashes white before the editor initializes. I am currently passing the state via 'ipcRenderer.send' to the new window. Should I pre-render the view?

Don't pre-render yet. Instead, update your 'Workbench' initialization sequence in 'workbench.ts' to stay hidden until the 'editorInitialized' event is emitted. Use 'win.hide()' by default and call 'win.show()' only after the React/DOM tree is populated to avoid the FOUC (Flash of Unstyled Content).

Good call. I've updated the 'Workbench' to await a 'ready-to-show' signal. Now, when I rip a tab out, the original window doesn't seem to remove the tab reference correctly, leaving an empty space where the tab was. How do I force the UI to recalculate the layout?

You need to trigger a layout refresh in your 'TabList' component. In 'tabList.ts', add a method 'refreshLayout()' that forces a re-render. Make sure you are removing the tab object from the global 'WindowManager' state before calling this method so that the 'TabList' doesn't attempt to render a null model.

It's working, but the window size of the new window feels inconsistent. When I drag a tab out, it defaults to the minimum size. I'd like it to match the dimensions of the tab that was ripped out. Can I pass the 'getBoundingClientRect' data through the IPC payload?

Yes, pass the 'width', 'height', and 'screenPosition' from the tab's DOM element as part of the 'drag-start' IPC message. In the main process, use 'new BrowserWindow({ x, y, width, height })' to instantiate the window exactly where the drag started.

I'm seeing a potential race condition where 'windowRegistry.ts' registers the new window before the previous window has finished its 'removeTab' operation. This is causing duplicate tabs in the global state. How should I sequence these IPC events?

Use a sequential command pattern. Don't let the main process create the new window until the source window sends a 'tab-removal-confirmed' message. This ensures the source is cleaned up and the 'WindowManager' state is consistent before the target window initializes.

The sequencing helped. Now, when dragging, the cursor icon is still the standard 'arrow' instead of the 'grab' or 'move' cursor. I've set 'cursor: grabbing' in the CSS, but it only applies to the element, not the window drag state.

That is because the 'grab' cursor is restricted to the browser context. To change it globally, you must use 'webContents.setCursor('grabbing')' in the main process when the drag starts. This will override the OS cursor for the duration of the proxy window's existence.
That worked! Now, what about accessibility? Drag and drop is notoriously hard for screen readers. Should I implement a keyboard-only alternative for ripping tabs?

Definitely. Add a command in 'commands.ts' called 'Move Tab to New Window'. This command can trigger a dialog or a quick-pick menu where the user can select the target window index or choose 'New Window'. It makes the functionality accessible to everyone.
The keyboard command is a great addition. One final issue: if I rip the last tab out of a window, the window stays open as an empty shell. Should I close the window automatically or keep it open?

Follow the 'Chrome' pattern: if it's the last tab in the window, close the window automatically. In your 'tabList.ts', check 'this.tabs.length === 0' after a drag event. If true, emit a 'close-last-tab' signal to the main process to terminate the window cleanly.
Implemented that check in 'tabList.ts'. The UX feels very close to a production browser now. Any performance concerns with keeping the 'windowRegistry.ts' monitoring all these window transitions?

The overhead of 'windowRegistry.ts' is negligible as long as you're using event-based updates rather than polling. Just ensure you unregister windows on the 'closed' event to prevent memory leaks in the 'WindowManager'. You've built a solid multi-window architecture for VS Code!

I noticed that when I close the last tab and the window shuts down, the VS Code process sometimes leaves behind a zombie instance of the Electron renderer. Is there a specific cleanup call I'm missing in the 'lifecycle.ts' module?

You are likely missing a explicit call to 'app.releaseExitCode()' or 'win.destroy()'. Since you are manually managing these windows, ensure 'windowRegistry.ts' triggers a proper 'app.quit()' check if the last window is gone, or at least calls 'win.close()' followed by 'win.webContents.destroy()' to force the renderer process to terminate.

That cleared the zombie processes! Now, I am testing tab reordering within the same window. The 'tabs.tsx' component uses a flex layout, but the drag-and-drop ghost element jitters when moving between adjacent tabs. Any advice on stabilizing the UI?

Flexbox layouts can be tricky for reordering. Try using a fixed width for each tab in 'tabs.tsx' during the drag session, or switch to a 'transform: translateX()' approach. By applying a CSS translate instead of modifying the document flow, you avoid triggering layout reflows that cause the jitter.

Using 'transform' definitely stopped the flickering. However, I noticed that saving a layout configuration in 'workspaceStorage.ts' is failing when I move tabs across windows. The JSON schema seems to struggle with identifying the window ID.

It's likely that the window ID changes or isn't serialized correctly. Ensure your 'workspaceStorage.ts' uses a stable persistent 'windowId' (a UUID) instead of the Electron-provided 'id' which resets on launch. Map the UUID to the current window instance in 'windowRegistry.ts'.

Mapping the UUID worked. Now, what about tab groups? If a user has a split-view inside a window, should 'ripping' the tab take the whole group or just the active file? The 'editorPart.ts' logic currently only grabs the active tab.

For a first implementation, stick to the active tab to keep the API stable. If you want to support group ripping, you would need to refactor 'editorPart.ts' to detect a group-drag event and serialize the entire 'TabGroup' object, which significantly increases complexity in your IPC payload.

Good point. Let's stick to the active tab for now. I'm seeing a flickering issue when the new window renders for the first time. It starts white for a split second before the theme is applied. How do I pre-load the theme in 'main.ts'?

In 'main.ts', you can pass the 'theme' key via the 'webPreferences' object during window creation. If you set 'backgroundColor' in the 'BrowserWindow' constructor options to match the theme's background color, you eliminate the white flash entirely during the renderer bootstrap phase.

Setting the 'backgroundColor' did the trick! Now, I want to allow users to merge windows by dragging a tab onto another window's title bar. How do I detect a drop event on the 'window frame' rather than just the tab strip?

You need to add a transparent overlay to the entire title bar in 'titleBar.tsx'. Use a 'drop-zone' class that listens for 'dragenter' events. If the event source is an external window, you can use 'ipcRenderer.send' to notify the main process to move the tab content.
The 'drop-zone' is working, but the drop target window doesn't gain focus. Should I be calling 'win.focus()' explicitly, or is that handled by the OS?

Electron's window management requires explicit calls. Inside your drop handler in the main process, call 'targetWindow.focus()' once the tab transfer is validated. If the window is behind others, use 'targetWindow.show()' or 'targetWindow.moveTop()' to ensure the user sees the result.
Everything is feeling smooth. Are there any edge cases with file dirty states? If I drag a dirty tab to another window, does 'workspaceStorage.ts' need to sync the buffer before the transfer?

Absolutely. You must call 'saveState()' or 'serializeBuffer()' in 'editorPart.ts' before the transfer completes. The safest way is to block the move until you get a 'confirmed-save' signal from the source window, ensuring the target window loads the exact content.
That seems robust. I'm now looking at the 'commands.ts' integration. Is it possible to add a 'Move to Next Window' hotkey that cycle-rotates tabs without needing to drag?

Yes, just create a command that retrieves the list of windows from 'windowRegistry.ts'. Use a simple index increment on the active window ID and then perform the same IPC transfer you wrote for the drag-and-drop feature. It's a great power-user feature.
Implemented the cycling hotkey. My tests in 'windowRegistry.test.ts' are failing because the window IDs are recreated in every test run. How do I mock the window registry correctly for unit tests?

Don't use the real 'WindowManager'. Use a stubbed version of the registry that returns fixed, predictable UUIDs. You can inject this via a constructor parameter in 'windowRegistry.ts' during test instantiation, allowing you to simulate multi-window state without triggering actual Electron events.
Mocking the registry solved the unit test flakiness. Last question: should I add a setting to enable/disable 'Tab Ripping' for users who dislike accidental drags?

Definitely. Add a new configuration entry in 'configuration.ts' called 'workbench.editor.enableTabDragging'. Default it to true, but allow users to set it to false. This makes the feature compliant with VS Code's user-first design principles.
Great suggestion. I'll add the configuration setting now. This project has been a massive learning experience for Electron-based IPC and window management. I'm ready to open the PR.

You've handled the architectural complexities of Electron windows perfectly. The implementation in 'windowRegistry.ts' and 'tabList.ts' is solid. Go ahead with the PR—just make sure your 'CONTRIBUTING.md' notes are updated if there are any specific local build flags needed for testing!

I noticed an issue during final integration in 'editorPart.ts'. When I move a tab with a long file path, the window title update lags behind the IPC response. Is there a race condition in the 'titleService.ts' update sequence?

That is likely due to the asynchronous nature of the window title event emission. Check if 'titleService.ts' is awaiting the 'EditorService.resolve()' promise before updating the UI state. You should wrap the title update in a batch-operation to prevent flickering during tab migration.

Good catch. Wrapping the call in a batch update in 'titleService.ts' resolved the flicker. Now, what about the 'tabBar.ts' focus state? When a tab is moved, the remaining tabs in the source window lose focus.

Focus management is tricky in Electron. Ensure you call 'focus()' on the next sibling in the DOM of 'tabBar.ts' after the removal event. Use a requestAnimationFrame to delay the focus call until the tab layout reflow completes.
Using requestAnimationFrame fixed the focus reset. I am now seeing an intermittent error in 'lifecycle.ts': 'Error: IPC channel closed' when closing the original window after dragging the last tab.

The error happens because the IPC listener is disposed before the final 'windowClose' event clears. You need to ensure the teardown sequence in 'lifecycle.ts' acknowledges all pending 'EditorSync' promises before allowing the window to destroy.
Added a promise-waiter to 'lifecycle.ts' and it cleaned up the logs. Is it feasible to support dragging multiple tabs at once by holding Shift, or is that too complex for this PR?

Keep this PR focused on single-tab dragging as per the requirement in issue #224. Multi-tab selection is a significant architectural change that requires updating the 'tabList.ts' selection model. Save that for a follow-up feature request.
Agreed. I'll stick to single tabs. I just ran a full suite of 'smoke-test.ts' and caught a regression where the 'pinned' status is lost during the move. How do I pass the metadata?

The 'TabModel' interface in 'tabList.ts' needs an updated serialization method. Ensure you include the 'isPinned' boolean property in the JSON payload transmitted over IPC. Check your 'serializable.ts' helper to ensure it correctly maps this field.
Updated 'serializable.ts' to include 'isPinned'. The metadata now carries over correctly, and the pinned state is preserved in the target window. This feels very stable now.
That is excellent news. Test the pinned state restoration across different window sizes to ensure the layout remains consistent. Does the target window correctly calculate the pinning margin?
Yes, it renders correctly. I noticed that dragging a tab into a window with no open editors causes a 'NullPointer' in 'editorGroup.ts'. I should add a check for an empty group.
Always initialize a default group if the target window is empty. Modify 'editorGroup.ts' to check 'group.isEmpty()' and instantiate the primary editor area before pushing the dropped tab metadata.
Added the safety check to 'editorGroup.ts'. The UX is much cleaner now. Should I add a logging event in 'telemetry.ts' to track how often users perform tab dragging?
Yes, adding a telemetry event for 'editor.tabDrag' is helpful for product owners to gauge feature adoption. Use the 'telemetryService.ts' provided in the core library and keep the payload anonymous.
Added the telemetry hook. I'm finalizing the docs in 'README.md' and double-checking the PR description. Any last security concerns regarding the IPC payload structure?

Validate the payload object in 'ipcHandler.ts' using a schema validator. Ensure that only expected fields like 'filePath' and 'pinned' are passed, preventing injection of malicious paths via intercepted IPC events.
Validated inputs against a strict schema. The implementation feels robust and secure. I am submitting the PR to the repository now!
Well done. You have navigated complex window management and IPC synchronization effectively. You are ready to push to the upstream branch. Good luck with the code review!
I've pushed the branch 'feature/tab-tearing' to the remote. The GitHub Actions CI just started, but I'm worried about the 'test-workbench-browser.ts' suite failing on Windows specifically.

Windows path normalization often causes issues in IPC serialization. Ensure you are using 'uri.ts' helpers to resolve the file paths before passing them through the 'tabManager.ts' IPC layer to avoid cross-platform discrepancies.
You are right. The test logs for 'test-workbench-browser.ts' show a 'URI mismatch' error. I am adjusting the normalization logic in 'ipcHandler.ts' to use 'URI.file()' consistently.

Good catch. Verify that 'URI.file()' handles UNC paths correctly on Windows, as those are notorious for breaking editor tab restoration. Check if 'paths.ts' utilities can assist with this normalization.
Applied the fix using 'paths.ts'. The browser tests are passing now, but I'm seeing a flickering effect in the tab bar when dragging in 'workbench-layout.css'. Is this a z-index issue?
It likely stems from a CSS transition on the 'tab-drag-ghost' element. Try setting 'pointer-events: none' on the ghost while dragging to prevent layout thrashing in 'workbench-layout.css'.
That fixed the flicker! I am now running the full integration suite locally. 'editor-group-test.ts' shows an intermittent failure where the editor doesn't focus after being dropped.

The focus management is handled in 'editorService.ts'. You might need to call 'focus()' on the editor instance after the 'onDidDrop' event fires. Ensure the promise resolves before attempting to focus.
Added an 'await' to the drop operation in 'editorService.ts'. The focus now transitions reliably to the newly ripped tab. Everything seems stable.
Great work. Before you consider this 'done', check if the tab-dragging feature respects the 'workbench.editor.closeEmptyGroups' setting in 'configuration.ts'. We shouldn't leave orphaned windows.
Excellent point. I've updated 'workbench.ts' to verify if the last tab was removed. If so, it will now automatically close the window if the setting permits it.
That handles the edge case perfectly. Your PR should now be clear of potential regression warnings. Did you update the 'constants.ts' file with the new feature flag?
I forgot the feature flag. Adding 'ENABLE_TAB_TEARING' to 'constants.ts' now and wrapping the new logic in a conditional check to ensure we can toggle it easily.
Smart move. Wrapping it in a feature flag allows for a canary release. Ensure the flag is default-true in 'settings.ts' so testers get the feature immediately.
Updated 'settings.ts'. I'm doing one final run through 'perf-test.ts' to ensure dragging tabs isn't causing memory leaks in the 'main-process.ts' IPC bridge.
Excellent diligence. Tab dragging involves a lot of object cloning; verify the Chrome heap snapshot in 'perf-test.ts' shows no steady growth after repeating the drag-and-drop cycle.
The memory usage looks flat. No leaks detected. I am confident in the implementation now. Finalizing the PR documentation and adding a changelog entry in 'CHANGELOG.md'.
You have thoroughly covered the implementation, stability, and UX aspects. Submit the final review and notify the maintainers of the 'feature/tab-tearing' branch.
Submitted! Awaiting feedback from the VS Code core team. This was a challenging but very rewarding feature to implement. Thanks for all the guidance.
It was a pleasure assisting you. You handled the architecture and edge cases like a pro. Keep an eye on those review comments; you're ready to get this merged.

I just received a notification from the maintainers. They are asking for a slight refactor. They want to move the tab-tearing logic from 'workbench.ts' into a new standalone service called 'TabManagerService' to improve maintainability.

That is a sound architectural request. Moving state management out of the main workbench ensures that your 'TabManagerService' can handle lifecycle events independently. Do you need help defining the interface for the service?
Yes, I need to define the 'ITabManagerService' in a new file 'tabManager.ts'. Should I inject the 'IWindowService' there to handle the cross-process communication for the window detachment?

Injecting 'IWindowService' is the standard approach for this in VS Code. Make sure you use the existing 'IInstantiationService' to register the service so that dependencies are correctly resolved during application boot.

I've drafted the 'TabManagerService' class. I am struggling with the 'teardown' phase when a tab is moved. Should I emit an 'onDidTabDetach' event, or is it better to rely on direct method invocation from 'workbench.ts'?

Using an event-driven approach via 'Emitter' is much cleaner. Your 'TabManagerService' should expose a public 'onDidTabDetach' event. This keeps the workbench loosely coupled to the service's internal state.

Good point. Implementing the 'Emitter' in 'tabManager.ts' now. Once I hook this into 'workbench.ts', I need to ensure that the drag-and-drop state in 'dnd.ts' remains synchronized with the new service.
Synchronizing 'dnd.ts' is critical. Ensure your drag-and-drop handler waits for the 'TabManagerService' to acknowledge the detachment before finalizing the mouse-up event to prevent race conditions.
I am currently seeing an 'IllegalStateException' in 'dnd.ts' when a drag occurs too quickly. It seems the service isn't initialized before the drag-end fires. I should probably add a guard clause.
A guard clause checking for 'this.tabManager.isInitialized' is definitely needed. Alternatively, you could use an async 'init' promise if the service startup takes time during the workbench load.
Good call. Adding a promise-based init flow to 'TabManagerService'. Running the integration suite now to verify that the drag-and-drop flow is correctly awaiting the service readiness.
While those tests run, have you checked if this refactor impacts the 'ENABLE_TAB_TEARING' flag in 'constants.ts'? Ensure the new service consumes that config during its own construction.
